key_terms.meaning: The software layer between the phone's hardware and its apps; it manages memory, power, security and app installation.
An open-source Linux-based mobile OS from Google, used by many phone makers; apps are written mainly in Java or Kotlin and run on ART.
Apple's closed-source mobile OS that runs only on Apple devices; apps come from the App Store and run in a strict sandbox.
Microsoft's tile-based mobile OS (2010 onward), now discontinued; it used the .NET/Silverlight model and its own Store.
Giving each app its own user ID and private data folder so it cannot read another app's files or memory.
A declared right to use a protected resource or API, such as CAMERA or INTERNET, granted by the user or at install time.
The engine that runs Android apps; it compiles app bytecode ahead of time or just in time and manages garbage collection.
The OS starts an app process when needed, keeps it while visible, and kills low-priority background processes when RAM runs short.
The OS suspends the CPU, radio and screen when idle, and bundles network and sensor work so the battery is not drained by many small wake-ups.
Software Development Kit: the libraries, compiler, emulator and debugging tools needed to build and install apps for one platform.
The official kit containing platform libraries (android.jar), build tools, the emulator, ADB and the documentation for each API level.
An integer that names one version of the Android platform; the manifest's minSdk and targetSdk choose which levels an app supports.
The build system used by Android Studio; it compiles code, merges resources and packages the APK or AAB.
Android Debug Bridge: a command-line tool that installs apps, shows logs and opens a shell on a device or emulator over USB or Wi-Fi.
The app's declaration file listing components, permissions, the launcher activity and SDK limits.
A class generated by the build tools that holds an integer ID for every resource, so Java code can refer to layout/main.xml as R.layout.main.
One screen of an app with its own window and life cycle, declared in the manifest and started by an intent.
The fixed order of callbacks onCreate, onStart, onResume, onPause, onStop and onDestroy as a screen appears, gets covered and closes.
A message object that carries an action, data and extras; it either names a component or asks the system to find one.
An intent that names the exact target component, for example new Intent(this, SecondActivity.class).
An intent that names only an action and data, such as ACTION_DIAL with a phone number, and the system matches it to a capable app.
A reusable piece of UI with its own life cycle that must live inside an activity and is managed by the FragmentManager.

takeaways: A mobile OS does four jobs that matter most to app developers: sandboxing, permissions, process and memory control, and power management.
Android, iOS and Windows Phone differed mainly in how open the platform was, how apps were distributed, and how strictly apps were sandboxed.
The Android platform is a stack of layers; the SDK lets you write code against one chosen API level of that stack.
An Android project is a small fixed set of files, and R is the generated bridge from Java code to XML resources.
An activity is one screen, and Android moves it through a fixed callback order as it becomes visible, gets covered and is destroyed.
Save your state in onSaveInstanceState and restore it in onCreate, because Android may recreate or kill your activity at any time.
An explicit intent names the activity to open; an implicit intent names an action and lets the system pick a handler.
A fragment lets one activity show different layouts for phone and tablet, and FragmentManager transactions add, replace and remove it.
bank_note: Long answers here are usually built on a labelled diagram plus the step-by-step callback order: the platform stack, the activity life cycle, and explicit versus implicit intents carry most of the marks.

bank.q: Explain the main functions of a mobile operating system. Compare Android, iOS and Windows Phone on app installation, updates and payment.
outline: Four core functions: sandboxing and permissions, process and memory management, power management, install/update/payment control
Android: open, multiple stores or sideloaded APK, Google Play billing, Play Protect scanning
iOS: single App Store, review process, in-app purchase via Apple, strong sandbox
Windows Phone: closed Microsoft Store, discontinued, smaller app ecosystem
Table or point-by-point comparison, then a short conclusion on openness versus control

bank.q: Draw the Android platform stack and explain the job of each layer from the Linux kernel up to the application layer.
outline: Six layers: Linux kernel, hardware abstraction layer, native C/C++ libraries, Android Runtime, application framework, applications
Kernel: drivers, process and memory management, power
HAL: standard interface between framework and driver code
Native libraries: SQLite, OpenGL ES, media, WebKit; ART: dex execution and garbage collection
Framework: Activity Manager, Package Manager, Content Providers, Views, Notification Manager
Application layer: user apps, each in its own sandbox

bank.q: Describe the Android activity life cycle with a diagram. State what work belongs in each callback.
outline: Callbacks in order: onCreate, onStart, onResume, onPause, onStop, onDestroy, plus onRestart
onCreate: inflate layout, bind views, restore saved state
onStart/onResume: screen visible, then interactive; acquire resources
onPause: release camera or sensors, save light state; still partly visible
onStop: heavy release, database cursors; onDestroy: final cleanup
Diagram shows the loop back from onPause to onResume when a dialog appears

bank.q: Explain the anatomy of an Android project. What is the R class and why is it generated rather than written by hand?
outline: Folders: app, java (or kotlin), res, Gradle scripts, AndroidManifest.xml
res split into layout, values (strings, colors), drawable, mipmap
Manifest declares components, launcher activity, permissions, SDK levels
Gradle builds the APK; two build types, debug and release
R is generated per build from resource names; gives an int ID for each resource
Ids change between builds, so hand-written constants would break; R also catches typos at compile time

bank.q: Compare explicit and implicit intents, with the manifest and code needed for each.
outline: Explicit: names component with class or ComponentName, used inside one app
Implicit: names action, data URI, category and extras, used to hand work to other apps
Example: new Intent(this, DetailActivity.class) versus ACTION_DIAL with tel: URI
Implicit intents are matched through intent filters in the target manifest
No match means ActivityNotFoundException, so check resolveActivity or wrap in try-catch
Security note: exported components and intent redirection

bank.q: Write the steps and code for an app with two screens: a button on the first screen opens the second and passes a student name. Show where each file goes.
outline: Two activities declared in AndroidManifest.xml, first one as launcher
Layout XML for each screen with a Button and a TextView
setContentView and findViewById in each onCreate
On click: Intent i = new Intent(this, SecondActivity.class); i.putExtra("name", value); startActivity(i)
In the second activity: getIntent().getStringExtra("name") and set it on the TextView
Mention back-stack behaviour and the Up button

bank.q: Write the code for an implicit intent that opens the dialer with a number, and for one that opens a map at a location. Explain how Android chooses the app.
outline: Dialer: Intent(Intent.ACTION_DIAL, Uri.parse("tel:" + number))
Map: Intent(Intent.ACTION_VIEW, Uri.parse("geo:0,0?q=..."))
System Package Manager looks up intent filters matching action and data
Zero matches give ActivityNotFoundException; several matches show a chooser
Intent.createChooser to force a chooser
ACTION_DIAL needs no permission; ACTION_CALL does

bank.q: Show how to build one activity that shows two fragments side by side in landscape and one at a time in portrait, using FragmentManager transactions.
outline: Two Fragment subclasses with their own layouts
Activity layout with a container FrameLayout or LinearLayout
FragmentManager fm = getSupportFragmentManager(); FragmentTransaction t = fm.beginTransaction()
t.replace(R.id.container, new ListFragment()); t.addToBackStack(null); t.commit()
List fragment calls back to the activity on item click; activity replaces the content fragment
Configuration check to pick layout, no duplicated activity logic
Use commitNow or commit; explain back-stack behaviour

bank.q: Android may kill a background activity process when memory runs low. Analyse how this affects app design and how state should be saved and restored.
outline: Process priority: foreground, visible, service, background, empty
Low-memory killer removes background processes first
onSaveInstanceState runs before the process can be killed; bundle of key-value data
onCreate receives the bundle; check for null
View state is saved automatically if the view has an id
Persistent data belongs in files, SharedPreferences or a database, not the bundle
Conclusion: treat the activity as easily recreated, not as long-term storage

bank.q: Analyse Android's sandbox and permission model as a security design. Where does it protect the user, and where can a careless developer weaken it?
outline: Each app gets a unique Linux user ID and a private data directory
Permissions declared in the manifest; dangerous ones granted at runtime since Android 6
Inter-process access only through declared, exported components
Weak points: over-broad permissions, exported activities and receivers, implicit intents leaking data, storing secrets in plain files, WebView settings
Mitigations: minimum permissions, signature permissions, HTTPS, scoped storage
Conclude with a balanced judgement, not a one-sided answer

bank.q: A team must support a phone and a large tablet from one codebase. Evaluate two activities and two layouts against a single activity with fragments, and recommend one.
outline: Two activities: simplest to write, duplicated logic, back-stack and state handling repeat
Fragments: modular, reusable, one activity holds list and detail in landscape, two activities or swapped fragments in portrait
Costs: fragment life cycle is more complex, transactions must be committed safely, communication through the activity
Criteria: code reuse, maintainability, back navigation, testing effort
Recommendation with a reason, and the case where the other choice wins

bank.q: Compare app distribution and payment in Android and iOS, and judge the effect on a small Indian developer building a UPI-based paid app.
outline: Android: Play Store plus other stores and direct APK; Play billing; fee on in-app purchases
iOS: single App Store with review; Apple in-app purchase rules
Android's larger low-cost device base in India; iOS higher average spend
Sideloading widens reach but raises piracy and malware risk
Rules that force one billing system limit choice of payment provider
Judgement: reach versus control, with a concrete recommendation

bank.q: A first app crashes every time the phone is rotated. Analyse the cause using the activity life cycle, and give two fixes.
outline: Rotation is a configuration change; Android destroys and recreates the activity by default
Any data held only in a local variable is lost; a null bundle or null view causes the crash
Fix 1: save values in onSaveInstanceState and read them in onCreate
Fix 2: keep data outside the activity, for example in a ViewModel or repository
Also mention android:configChanges as a workaround, with its drawbacks
Mention that onDestroy is called, so unregister listeners there

glossary.def: An isolated area of storage and memory that only one app's user ID can read or write.
Android Package: the installable file that holds an app's code, resources and manifest.
Installing an app from a file or non-official store instead of the main store.
A marketplace that distributes apps and collects payment for paid apps and in-app purchases.
Automatic freeing of memory that no longer has a live reference, done by the runtime.
The Android component that closes low-priority background processes when RAM is short.
A power-saving mode that delays background network and CPU work when the phone is idle and still.
An integer identifying one version of the Android platform and its available classes.
The lowest API level on which the app will install and run.
The API level the app was tested against, which turns on that version's behaviour changes.
Android Virtual Device: an emulated phone or tablet, with a chosen API level, that runs on your computer.
The build tool that compiles code, merges resources and produces the APK or app bundle.
The XML file that declares an app's components, permissions and required SDK levels.
An integer generated into R that names one layout, string, drawable or view.
The handle an app uses to reach its resources, package information and system services.
The first activity callback, where you inflate the layout and set up state.
The callback when the activity loses focus but may still be partly visible.
The callback where an activity stores small pieces of state in a Bundle before it may be killed.
The stack of activities or fragment transactions that the Back button pops.
Key-value data carried inside an intent's Bundle to the receiving component.
A manifest entry that declares which actions, data types and categories a component can handle.
A wrapped intent that another app may fire later on your app's behalf, used in notifications and alarms.
The object that adds, replaces, removes and tracks fragments inside an activity.
A fragment that shows a floating dialog window instead of a full screen.
